speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: Well, let's see… you and Edward graduating eighth grade that year, that's pretty much it. Yeah. Dad would come to Kendrick to get work for four of us boys. He told me the reason. And he'd come down here... How much money was it? I told you that before, didn't I? He wouldn't come unless he bought this house. And I think he cleaned up $500, $1 ,500, and he put $500 payment on this house. And he went down to town and he bought out a wetsuit shop for $500. He bought out a dray team and dray line for $500. He could give all good dealing with four boys. He'd come down there and... Well, it was four boys and he had work for all of them but me and he'd farm me out.

Kids never got a chance to come in and pick out anything. We always did, though. We had our own money and we'd done our own buying.

He said, we couldn't have Ed, but they could have me. He wasn't very anxious to harm any… worked first month… started work for, what, $30 a month? I think it was. But I got to raise the first month. words: Tape. Well, them days the trains always carried the passenger trains. The last car was the, what do you call them… observation. Observation cars. And they had a platform in the back, you know, where you could go out and look. The country coming through, or you could get a train stopped right there. So he, when he comes through, he comes out of the car onto this weekend. We're in the train, start giving his speech, and he's about half asleep, he's sounding like it. He says,… when I come up through this beautiful valley of yours and... He's touching it. And all the fruit trees and everything, I don't think he ever looked out, because he wouldn't meet many fruit trees during here in the most. And this time there's one big orchard to ride out of us. And... And he says it. He just made me feel like a big red apple.

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: Here's a big pot of gunpowder. You've seen a picture of him, you know? That's why I just feel like a big red apple. Speaking of presidents, what I remember most about seeing a president with Theodore Roosevelt come to Moscow, and of course, he let out, and let everybody go that could go up to share him. And... And we heard him speak on top of that. He had a great big... For as reason as his father, he brought a great big stack of wheat and sacks, you know, sack wheat. And I can remember that in his pal, and that is the platform he's speaking. He spoke from this platform, that Roosevelt did. That's what I remember about him. Yeah, you know.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: Did you ride the train up? Is that how you got up there?

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: Yeah, oh sure… we went to Moscow more than we did to... And he... And then, listen, because we could go up to Moscow in the morning on the 9 o 'clock, and come back at the night train, you know, and you could have a whole day up there. You'd be back down there about 9 o 'clock, the train just coming, like 9, 10 o 'clock. But coming to Lewiston, you know, up here, they'd come up on 9 o 'clock. Well, there's a lot of... quite a few people coming, the Indians come train, but unless they waited for the night train, they'd have to go back over here about 12 o 'clock to catch the train going back. There's one come up at 4 o 'clock in the evening.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: Wouldn't cost very much, would it, to ride to Moscow?

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: Well, I think... I think it's a little less than a dollar, if I remember right. It's a round dollar, pretty close to a dollar.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: So you still didn't do it real often?

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: Oh, I'm turning right you didn't do it real often. You didn't have the money to do a lot of things real often. You know, but them days it's different. Now, if you wait till you need a pair of shoes, you're going to buy a pair of shoes. And if you wait till you need a shirt, you're going to buy a shirt. But in them days, you went and bought your two seasons, you bought a clothes. You fixed up for the fall and you fixed up for the summer, spring. And that's... that was the end of our shopping. It wasn't any more shopping than buying… yeah… we had... most people, kids I run with and everything got all their stuff from mailer house, but gosh, we never had any luck buying from mailer house. If we bought anything, we'd have sent it back, wouldn't fit or something. Gosh. I know one time mother, of course, did her own stuff for us in the fall. She only tried it once.

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: I don't think they do the mailer business they used to do.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: Oh, it's pretty big.

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: Is it… yeah… didn't tell them for talks. Yeah. Well, no, but they didn't like it. It was no mistake.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: You can't get as many different things. You can't get... They sold, you know, they sold up to wagons down tools and everything, you know, they don't...

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: They don't anymore, huh?

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: Not as much as that, I don't know.

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: Well, they sold that, and they ate too. Yeah.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: What was the story about the blacksmith when you were a little boy?

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: A fellow named Hodges used witter and the wood dark place. And I used to stick around, we were pretty good pals. I was just a kid. And give me a job, I'd make it. Them days there was a lot of wagon and hack work, you know, tightening up wheels. They made wedges, I don't know what they called them. Well, it was a wheel, wedges for spokes, wedges for spokes, you know, after they put spokes in, you know, on the rim. They put them wedges in there, tighten it before they put the... What do you call them? Tire. Steel tire. You know, you used to go over there and make these hardwood wedges. Oh. The hands, you know, it's so... Some blocks, and I'd make it with that. I'd draw a knife, I'd make these wedges. Hardwood wedges. He'd pay me with a hundred.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: How many would you make in a day?

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: Oh, I don't know. I don't remember that. I made quite a few. I made them until I got tired. Oh, I made a hundred maybe. Maybe two hundred, I don't remember.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: You were still in Leland then, right?

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: Yeah, weirdly. Well, I was an old kind of business. What about the clothes that man made that black slip? Oh, yeah. He was always made... He was a clown. And he'd black himself up, you know. He was really a clown. He was a good one, too. But he made this doll, wooden doll, and jointed the legs and the arms. And he put this thing on a board after he made it, and he had a whole board in the back of it, you know, and a handle put on him. So he'd hold this. He'd hold it with one hand out on this board, and he'd pound it, make a batch with it. We'd hit it in the board, you know, hammer or something, maybe. And he'd make that thing, oh boy, he'd really make that thing dance. That was cute. It was really short. He was always clowning. He was a character.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: He liked kids?

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: Oh, he loved them. He all loved him, too. He didn't have any kids of his own... Oh, yeah. He was grown, married. He married one... Finally, I don't know whether he was married before he come to Lille or not. He was a pastor then, but he married one of the Huffman girls up here on the hill. Yeah, he died. She died. She died, and he never got married again after that. Gee, I think there isn't any names or any people left up there anymore. All them people used to be around Lille. There's not much there. One or two farmers owned it all.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: What all was in Leland when you lived there? What businesses?

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: It would be easier to tell you what business wasn't there. ... Well, there was a big General store, and it was the biggest anything in Kendrick. He went in to Gosford, and one time there was two hardwares up there, but there was always a hardware store. They sold machinery, and then there was a drug store and a butcher shop. We had the butcher shop and a big General store. Sometimes there was another store, but the only one that you went in to Gosford was one that really mad the business and made it there. They made a pile of money there. And the floor mill. They made floor there. Van Pelt Mill. You've probably heard of that. Yeah.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: You told us about his phone.

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: His telephone. Yeah. That's the reason he had this phone to keep the market on the wheat. Was there a barber shop… yeah. One time… doctors… dentist… two saloon at one time... Two churches at one time. The UB Church never got started hardly. It never got going there. There's South Methodist and North Methodist. Democrats on one side of the street and the Republicans on the other. That's a fact.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: Which one were you going to?

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: What did he think? I'll let you set your mind on it. My dad had turned over in his grave if he was going over to North Methodist Church. See the north and south. One was on South Sides Street and the other. One was on the north. One catered to niggas and the other didn't. Didn't have any niggers. That's right though. All the Republicans down there at the NE North Church. South Methodist, all Democrats. Well, I guess just the same way it is yet, ain't it?

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: North and South is. Well, it's changing. I bet it isn't back. Not as straight. Not in the south, I bet it ain't changing. They're still Democrats. I'll say they're Democrats. They don't get a vote and they'll see where they're elected to you.

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: What do you think of our president? Is he going to make it again? I don't know. It's kind of shaky.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: Who's going to run and catch him?

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: I don't know. I'm waiting for Senator Church. Well, I know, but he won't... Church will be on Democratic ticket. Well, he won't have no trouble in the primary, Mr… president, will he?

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: Well, they're not even sure about that. He was pretty close in New Hampshire. When you were a kid.

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: When I first came to Kendrick, there was a post office at Bleelyn, one at Cameron, one at Southwick, one at... Did I say... one at Cabbany's and one at Teakean. How many is that? One… five… at Teakean. And then there was... Lyndon and Crescent and Park. There was three more… is that eight… is that it? Then there was all post offices.

speaker: Lee Magnusen
words: Were those little ones, like in somebody's house?

speaker: F. Marvin Long or Martha Lowery Long
words: Yeah, they were all packed in that house. Some places were there. A store and them places.
